newsitem.title: UK: Base metals are the latest commodity to rally.
newsitem.headline: Base metals are the latest commodity to rally.

text.p: Industrial metals prices edged higher on Thursday in the latest speculative rally in world commodity markets.
Gold hovered some way above recent 3-3/4 year lows from which it had made a spectacular bounce on Wednesday but dealers said its prospects were uncertain.
Oil prices eased while coffee futures extended a dramatic advance in New York but ended slightly down in London.
In the industrial metals, copper, aluminium and zinc all had a robust day on the London Metal Exchange on tight nearby supply and speculative buying.

Zinc climbed to fresh two-year peaks, copper came within a whisker of regaining the significant psychological threshold of $2,300 per tonne and aluminium wrapped up the day by wiping out more corrective losses.
Three months copper closed the afternoon at $2,275 per tonne, up $25, but well off the morning high of $2,295.

Floor traders earlier said data on LME warehouse stocks of copper on Friday was expected to be level to 3,000 tonnes higher, but another trader said later inventories may rise by as much as 7,000 tonnes.

Zinc gained $35 or three percent on the day to end at $1,221 after fund buying propelled it above $1,200 in the morning, which in turn triggered stops and fuelled more speculative and technical buying.
Aluminium got a boost from Chinese buying, sending it to a peak of $1,578. The market ended just $2 off the high, a gain on the day of $21.
The market has rebounded strongly since bottoming on Tuesday at $1,534 in what analysts called a correction to a four-month uptrend.
In bullion markets, gold had risen almost $10 in an hour on Wednesday to trade above $345 an ounce, after it had sunk as low as $336.50 in early European business.
Thursday saw it just easier at $341.85 by the London close in a market that dealers said was consolidating after Wednesday's gyrations.
New York futures for Arabica coffee climbed to fresh contract highs.
March Arabica futures hit 177.25 cents per pound in the rally that has already worked through to firmer retail prices in Europe and the United States and may have further to go.

But London Robusta type coffee futures were less buoyant and ended easier, down $7.0 per tonne. The rally on coffee has been based on low stocks and concerns about supply from Brazil, where the crop may be lower than had been expected, and from strike-hit Colombia.
Crude oil eased under the weight of ample supply. Grains were active but within recent ranges.
